comparison: Perfect agreement on methodological claims (C2, C85-C112). Both evaluations rate the study design as SUPPORTED, with peer reviewers explicitly praising it as 'exceptionally well-designed' and OpenEval noting the 'methodologically sound' stratified sampling approach. Both acknowledge the successful decorrelation of habitat loss and fragmentation per se as a major strength.

Strong agreement on correlational findings (C30-C34). Both evaluations rate these claims as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes the findings are 'statistically supported with reported effect sizes' while acknowledging correlations don't establish causation. Peer reviewers accepted these findings without critique, affirming the differential effects of habitat loss versus fragmentation per se.

Agreement on multi-model averaging results (C37-C43). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes the appropriate methodology and stronger plant diversity effects than direct landscape effects. Peer reviewers accepted these findings and praised the study for providing 'compelling evidence' regarding how landscape context affects BEF relationships, also accepting the indirect pathways (C60-C61, C69).

Agreement on SEM analysis (C3-C5, C48, C52-C55). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes adequate model fit statistics and methodologically sound identification of indirect pathways, while cautioning about assumed directionality. Peer reviewers accepted the SEM results without methodological critique and praised the analysis of 'complex ecological relationships.'

Strong agreement on modulation analysis and specialist mechanism (C6-C7, C44-C47, C49-C51, C72-C73, C75). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval highlights consistent patterns across regression and SEM with visual demonstration in Figure 4. Peer reviewers explicitly highlighted this as a key contribution, noting the role of specialists in shaping BEF relationships as 'another strength.'

Disagreement on nonlinear fragmentation effects (C46-C47, C79-C80). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting mixed statistical evidence with non-significant regression results (p>0.05) contradicting visual patterns. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting Figure 4 patterns without challenge and not questioning the mechanistic explanations involving edge effects.

Agreement on main synthetic conclusions (C8-C9). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes convergent evidence across multiple analytical approaches. Peer reviewers explicitly affirmed these conclusions about inconsistent effects of habitat loss versus fragmentation per se. However, OpenEval R7 covers broader claims (C56-C57, C60-C61, C69-C77) while peer R7 focuses on core conclusions and conservation implications (C58, C78).

Partial disagreement on management recommendations (C58, C78). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting these extend beyond data to predictive/prescriptive claims requiring additional validation. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting conservation implications and noting the work 'has important implications for ecosystem restoration.' OpenEval is more cautious about extrapolation beyond empirical findings.

Agreement on fragmentation metric interpretation caveat (C59). Both evaluations support this claim. OpenEval rates the broader set (C58-C59, C78) as UNCERTAIN but notes C59 'appropriately cautions about interpretation.' Peer reviewers explicitly accepted this clarification, noting authors provided detailed information about fragmentation indices' ecological significance.

Disagreement on mechanistic interpretations (C62-C65, C68). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, characterizing these as 'largely speculative' and 'post-hoc rationalization' supported by citations rather than direct measurements, requiring direct testing. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED, accepting edge effect mechanisms and environmental pathways without challenge, noting approvingly the integration of soil water and temperature controls.

Disagreement on edge effect and heterogeneity mechanisms (C81-C82). OpenEval rates these as UNCERTAIN within broader mechanistic claims (C62-C68, C81-C82), noting they are speculative and not directly measured. Peer reviewers rate as SUPPORTED within their evaluation of nonlinear patterns (C79-C82), accepting mechanistic explanations involving spatial asynchrony and edge effects without critique.

OpenEval evaluated background and literature review claims (C10-C28, C83-C84) as SUPPORTED, noting they appropriately summarize prior literature and establish theoretical framework. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these background claims, as peer reviewers focused on empirical findings and study design rather than literature contextualization.

Overlap on differential effects summary (C56-C57). OpenEval R7 includes these in broader synthetic conclusions rated as SUPPORTED. Peer R2 also addresses these claims as part of accepting differential effects of habitat loss versus fragmentation, rating as SUPPORTED. Both evaluations agree on these summary findings.

Overlap on indirect pathway conclusions (C60-C61, C69). OpenEval R7 includes these in synthetic conclusions rated as SUPPORTED, emphasizing convergent evidence. Peer R3 implicitly accepts these claims when affirming the study's findings about how landscape affects BEF through indirect pathways, rating as SUPPORTED.

Overlap on specialist mechanism conclusions (C71, C74, C76-C77). OpenEval R7 includes these in broader synthetic conclusions rated as SUPPORTED. Peer R5 explicitly addresses the specialist mechanism as a key contribution, rating as SUPPORTED and highlighting it as 'another strength' of the study.
